## Has R&B Shifted from Danceable to Atmospheric?

This project set out to answer one question: has R&B shifted from a danceable, movement-oriented style to a more atmospheric and introspective one? Across five analytical sections, the answer is consistent and clear.

```{=html}
<div style="
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #2D1B69, #1a0a3d);
  border-left: 4px solid #FF2D78;
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 1.2rem 1.5rem;
  margin: 1.5rem 0;
  font-size: 1.1rem;
  font-weight: 600;
  color: white;
">
  Yes. The shift is measurable, and it runs deep across every dimension of the music examined.
</div>
```

## Summary of Findings

| Section | 1990s R&B | 2020s R&B | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Track-level features | High danceability, energy, valence, loudness | Lower and more variable on all features | Shifted toward less rhythmic intensity and more subdued emotional tone |
| Chroma | Few repeating pitch classes, tight harmonic loops | Wider pitch class distribution, tonal ambiguity | Moved from harmonic stability to harmonic openness |
| Temporal | Narrow tempo range, longer tracks, stable pulse | Broader tempo variation, shorter tracks, looser pulse | Less rhythmically consistent, more structurally flexible |
| Timbre | Dense timbral profiles, clear section repetition | Softer, more uniform timbre, continuous form | From layered active production to restrained atmospheric texture |
| Clustering | Clusters around high energy and danceability | Clusters around high acousticness, era separable by kNN | The two eras occupy distinct regions of the audio feature space |

## Feature Comparison

| Feature | 1990s | 2020s |
|---|---|---|
| Danceability | High, consistent (peak ~0.75) | Lower, more spread |
| Energy | High | Moderate, more variable |
| Valence | High positivity | More subdued, wider range |
| Loudness | Louder, more compressed | Quieter on average |
| Acousticness | Low | Higher |
| Harmonic stability | Tonally stable, one key | Harmonically mobile |
| Track duration | Longer | Shorter |
| Rhythmic density | Dense, regular pulse | Gradual, less dominant pulse |

## Who Could Benefit?

These findings have practical relevance beyond academic musicology.

**Streaming platforms** could use era-based feature profiles to improve how R&B is surfaced and recommended, distinguishing between tracks designed for collective energy and those designed for personal atmosphere. A listener playing 1990s groove-driven R&B has different needs than one playing late-night SZA and the data shows those needs map onto measurable audio differences.

**Music educators** might find this a useful demonstration of how quantitative methods can complement close listening and cultural analysis. The project shows students that computational tools are not a replacement for interpretation, but a way to make patterns visible before asking what they mean.

**Artists and producers** working in R&B today could use this kind of analysis to understand where the genre has moved and make more deliberate choices about where their own work sits within it. The feature profiles give a precise picture of what has changed and what has been left behind.

**Music journalists and critics** could draw on this approach to ground stylistic claims in data, moving beyond impressionistic descriptions of genre evolution toward arguments that are testable and specific.

## Limitations

The corpus is small, with 25 tracks per era, meaning individual tracks can have an outsized effect on distributional results. The boundaries of R&B are porous and several tracks carry influences from pop, hip-hop, and soul. Spotify's audio features are algorithmic estimates rather than ground truth measurements and may not capture every dimension of musical expression. These limitations do not undermine the findings but mean the results should be understood as suggestive rather than definitive.

## What I Learned?

This project taught me that computational methods are most powerful when their results converge. Any single analysis a boxplot of danceability, a chroma heatmap, a dendrogram could be dismissed as a quirk of the data or an artefact of Spotify's algorithms. But when five independent analyses all point in the same direction, the pattern becomes harder to ignore. Learning to read that kind of convergence, and to trust it, was the most important methodological lesson of this project.

I also learned that numbers do not explain themselves. The data showed that 2020s R&B is quieter, less danceable, and more acoustic than its 1990s counterpart. But it took close listening, cultural context, and careful interpretation to understand what that actually means: a genre shifting from collective to private experience, from the body to the mood. Computational musicology works best when it moves between the quantitative and the qualitative, using each to check and enrich the other.

Finally, I learned something about R&B itself. I came into this project with an intuition that something had changed in the genre, but I did not expect the shift to be so consistent across every dimension of the music. The fact that era alone predicts cluster membership that a kNN classifier trained on audio features can tell 1990s from 2020s R&B with meaningful accuracy suggests the change is not superficial. It is structural, and it is real.

## Final Reflection

What this analysis ultimately suggests is that R&B has not only changed in sound, but in purpose. The genre has moved from a music designed to be felt collectively, in the body and on the dancefloor, toward a music designed to be felt privately, in the mind and in the mood. Whether that shift reflects changes in technology, culture, listening habits, or simply what people need from music at different moments in history is a question that goes beyond the data. But the data makes one thing clear: the shift has happened, and it is audible in every dimension of the music examined here.
